title: Entertaining angels (Hebrews 13:1–2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long list of the faithful in Hebrews eleven. Your line was faith is the substance. Whose name did you add to the list? Day six hundred three.

The hottest part of the day. An old man sits at the door of his tent, under the oaks of Mamre, and looks up to see three strangers standing nearby. He doesn't wait to find out who they are. He runs to meet them, bows to the ground, and has bread baked and a calf prepared, while they rest in the shade. That's Abraham in Genesis eighteen, and by the end of the visit it's clear these were no ordinary travelers. Centuries later, the letter to the Hebrews is nearly finished. The big arguments are over. And in its last chapter, among a few short pieces of advice, the writer reaches back for that afternoon.
screen: `THREE STRANGERS AT MAMRE.` → `ABRAHAM RUNS TO MEET THEM.` → `HEBREWS REMEMBERS THAT AFTERNOON.`

segments.voice: Chapter thirteen begins with two kinds of love, side by side. First, love for the family of believers. Then love for people you don't know at all. The Douay-Rheims puts it this way: "And hospitality do not forget; for by this some, being not aware of it, have entertained angels." The King James Bible ends the verse with the phrase in today's line: angels unawares. The Greek word behind hospitality is philoxenia, which is simply love of strangers. Not love of guests you invited. Love of the person you didn't expect. Hebrews names no one here, but readers often think of stories like these. Abraham at Mamre, feeding three visitors. Lot, taking two strangers into his house in Sodom. And Catholic Bibles hold another one, in the book of Tobias: a young man sets out on a long journey with a hired companion who calls himself Azarias, and only at the very end does the companion reveal that he is the angel Raphael. A whole road trip, and nobody knew. Notice what Hebrews doesn't say. It doesn't promise that every stranger is an angel, or tell you to be kind in case one is. The point runs the other way: you can't sort people in advance, so welcome everyone. Jesus says it even more directly in Matthew twenty-five: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." Saint Benedict wrote it into his rule for monks: every guest who comes to the door is to be received as Christ himself.
screen: `PHILOXENIA: LOVE OF STRANGERS.` · `ABRAHAM, LOT, TOBIAS AND RAPHAEL.` · `YOU CAN'T SORT PEOPLE IN ADVANCE.` · `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YOU TOOK ME IN.` · then, large: `ANGELS UNAWARES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome a stranger, starting in your mind. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone new to a place you know: a new face at work or at church, a family that just moved onto your street, someone who looked lost the last time you saw them. Picture them at the edge of the room. Now picture yourself crossing it to greet them, and making room for them at the table. Let that feel ordinary. If you pray, you can hold the line, I was a stranger, and you took me in, and ask to notice the next stranger. If you don't, just hold the face kindly. The bell holds the time.
Entertaining angels. Hebrews thirteen: welcome strangers, because some, without knowing it, have welcomed angels. Today's word.
Your line: angels unawares. Today, welcome one stranger properly: hold a door, make room at a table, say hello first. Day six hundred three.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes, religious houses and charities practice hospitality to strangers, from welcoming newcomers at Mass to meals and shelter for travelers and the homeless, and Benedictine monasteries still receive guests as Christ, following the Rule of Saint Benedict.

notes: Douay-Rheims Hebrews 13:2: confirm exact punctuation ('do not forget; for by this some, being not aware of it, have entertained angels').
The carry 'angels unawares' is the King James phrasing; the script names the KJV as the source of the phrase. Confirm this is acceptable on the Catholic path.
Abraham, Lot and Raphael (Tobias 5 and 12) are given as stories readers would have thought of; the script says plainly that Hebrews names no one here.
Raphael's alias Azarias (Tobias 5:18 in Douay-Rheims numbering; 5:12 in some modern Bibles). Confirm.
Rule of Saint Benedict ch. 53: all guests received as Christ. Paraphrased.
Philadelphia in Hebrews 13:1 and philoxenia in 13:2: confirm the Greek pairing.
